newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU wants diplomatic weight to match economic clout.
newsitem.headline: EU wants diplomatic weight to match economic clout.

text.p: The European Union, tired of seeing the United States step in to sort out foreign policy crises on its own doorstep, wants to develop a world diplomacy to match its unquestionable economic might.

"Europeans," French President Jacques Chirac said this week, "will have an impact on world affairs only if they know how to combine their efforts within the framework of shared and ambitious foreign and defence policies."
But plans by negotiators on a new EU treaty to forge such policies have fallen short of what many in the bloc hoped for.

EU leaders, meeting at a summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday to agree the treaty, are likely to take modest steps towards improving the bloc's role in foreign policy and make hardly any headway on a common defence policy.
On defence, no one argues that the EU can or should take NATO's place as the West's primary military arm.

But France, Germany, Italy and others had hoped to incorporate the Western European Union (WEU) defence group fully into the bloc as a way of underlining its intention to become a political as well as an economic union.
The idea, however, has been scuppered by Britain, Denmark and the neutral EU states, Sweden, Finland, Ireland and Austria.
Instead of setting a timetable for WEU integration, the new treaty is likely to reiterate what is already in the EU treaty -- that the grouping will one day be a defence arm for the bloc.
The treaty, however, will define the EU's defence policy as involving peacekeeping and humanitarian tasks.

More progress is expected on the foreign policy front, with the new treaty likely to create an EU foreign policy chief, a foreign policy forward planning unit, and a system under which EU leaders will identify foreign policy objectives for the bloc to act as guideposts for dealing with crises when they erupt.

French plans for a high-profile foreign policy supremo have been toned down, but the new coordinator, with the rank of secretary general, could be the key player in a new "troika" for dealing with the EU's external presence.

Under one plan, the current troika of the foreign ministers of the past, present and future EU presidencies, would be replaced by one comprising the secretary general, the European Commission president and the current EU presidency minister.
Critics of the bloc's current foreign policy performance had hoped that decisions would be taken by majority vote, stopping one country from blocking the rest from acting.

Going into the summit, however, it appears unlikely that the national veto would be wrested away from countries keen to keep their sovereign place in the world -- although there will be consideration of a system for abstaining.
